_comment: Shared cross-language corpus for resolving a venue-local WALL CLOCK to an
instant (PSY-2024).
THE CONTRACT: a wall clock a person typed into the show form must resolve to
the same instant the Go writers resolve it to, on every night of the year,
including the two nights a zone's clocks move. A frontend that resolves a
transition-night clock differently stores a time nobody entered, and no read
surface can tell that instant from a correct one.
Go reads this file in utils.TestDSTClockCorpus, which asserts every row is
what time.Date produces. TypeScript reads the same file twice, in
frontend/lib/utils/timeUtils.test.ts, which asserts every row is what
combineDateTimeToUTC produces, and in cli/test/timezone.test.ts, which
asserts every row is what localTimeToUTC and localClockExists produce.
Neither language owns the numbers: the Go run
checks every one against time.Date, so a row nobody can reproduce fails that
suite rather than sitting here as a claim.
WHAT THIS PINS, exactly. The Go side holds time.Date, which is the function
the Go writers call (pipeline.venueLocalInstant, community.parseShowEventDate,
catalog.reanchorEventDate all compose through it), not those writers
themselves: a writer that stopped calling time.Date would not fail here. The
TypeScript side holds the two resolvers themselves: the frontend's and the
ph CLI's in cli/src/lib/timezone.ts.
FIELDS
date, clock, zone = the wall clock a source or a form field states.
utc      = the instant time.Date(y, m, d, h, min, 0, 0, loc) returns for it.
exists   = whether that instant reads back in the zone as the clock asked
for. False only inside the hour (or half hour) a spring-forward
skips, where there is no correct answer and every implementation
still has to return something. The show form asks this before
storing. The Go writers do not, and the create/update API cannot:
it takes event_date as an already-parsed instant, which no longer
carries the wall clock that produced it (see the note on
utils.DateOnlyEventHour).
ambiguous= the clock happens TWICE, in the overlap a fall-back creates.
Which of the two instants is returned varies by zone: it is
whichever side the offset probe lands on, so 01:30 on
America/Chicago's fall-back night resolves to the FIRST
occurrence and 02:30 on Europe/Berlin's resolves to the SECOND.
Agreement with time.Date is the whole rule; 'the first one' is
not, and stating it as one would be false for half these rows.
why      = which case in the transition the row is buying.
Rows carrying a zone this runtime cannot load fail loudly rather than being
skipped, so both suites embed or assume a full IANA database.
